Trencsen
tren'chayn
n. (Upper Hungarian county town on the Vag, Slovak Trencin; a Protestant centre of the north-west until the Jesuit settlement of 1655)
Hungarian Trencsen, Slovak Trencin, from a Slavic root, the name recorded in antiquity as Laugaricio on the castle rock above the Vag.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Trencsen stands under a castle on the Vag in the north-west of old Hungary, on the road from Moravia, and that road made its church history. The Reformation reached it early from the Moravian and Silesian side, the county nobility took it, and for a century the town was one of the centres from which the Lutheran church of the Slovak-speaking counties was supplied with ministers and books. The Synod of Zsolna, which organised that church, was held thirty miles away under the protection of the Thurzo family, whose seat was the county. Trencsen also received the refugees the other way: Bohemian and Moravian exiles after 1620 came down the same road, and the town's printing and preaching were strengthened by men who had lost everything in the Habsburg settlement of their own country. From 1655 the balance turned, a Jesuit college was established in the town, the magistracy was pressed, and over two generations Trencsen became a Catholic county seat with a Protestant minority. The dictionary enters it as a plain case of the Counter-Reformation's actual method in Hungary, which was not usually the scaffold: it was a college, a patron, a lawsuit over a church building, and fifty years of patience.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a refugee as one who flees to a place of safety; a seminary as a place of education; and patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm mind.

expand to see more

REFUGEE, n. [Fr. refugie.] One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country.

SEMINARY, n. [L. seminarium, a seed-plot.] A place of education; any school, academy, college or university in which young persons are instructed.

PATIENCE, n. [L. patientia.] The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.

PATRON, n. One who countenances, supports or protects; a guardian; an advocate; one who has the gift of a church living.

LAWSUIT, n. An action in law for the recovery of a supposed right; a process in law instituted by a party to compel another to do him justice.

Key Scripture

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

1Pe 2:11 — "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;"

Jam 5:11 — "Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy."

Gal 6:9 — "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."

Modern Corruption

North-western Hungarian county seat, a Protestant centre strengthened by Moravian exiles, which a Jesuit college and fifty years of pressure turned Catholic.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the Counter-Reformation's patient method, which is more instructive than its violent one. In Hungary, outside the crises of the 1670s and 1687, the old religion was recovered chiefly by founding schools the Protestants could not match, converting or replacing the landlord who held the right of presentation, and litigating over the ownership of church buildings until the Protestant congregation was worshipping in a barn. There is no scaffold in that account and it was far more effective than the scaffold. A church that prepares itself only against persecution will be taken apart by a school and a lawyer.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is perseverance in the ordinary. “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) is the answer to a fifty-year campaign, and the answer is not a counter-campaign but a church that keeps teaching its children, training its ministers and holding its ground through three generations of discouragement.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parepidemos (G3927), a sojourner, a resident alien; Greek hupomone (G5281), patient endurance.

expand to see more

Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, a foreigner; “they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth”, Hebrews 11:13.

Greek aspazomai (G782) — to greet, to embrace, to welcome; “and embraced them”, Hebrews 11:13.

Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a sojourner in a strange land; “as strangers and pilgrims”, 1 Peter 2:11.

Greek hupomeno (G5278) — to endure, to bear up under; “we count them happy which endure”, James 5:11.

Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to lose heart, to grow weary; “let us not be weary in well doing”, Galatians 6:9.

Usage

"“they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) — Bohemian and Moravian exiles coming down the Vag road after 1620."

"“Behold, we count them happy which endure” (Jam 5:11) — two generations of pressure after the Jesuit settlement of 1655."

"“let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) — the answer to a method that worked by patience."
